result.summary: The poet asks the Muse to sing of the mother of all gods and men, who delights in rattles, timbrels, flutes, the cries of wolves and lions, and the echoing wooded hills. He closes by greeting her and all goddesses.

scenes.title: Invocation to the Mother
scenes.summary: The poet calls on the Muse to sing of the Mother of the gods, describes what pleases her, and bids her and all goddesses hail.

characters.name: Muse
characters.description: clear-voiced daughter of Zeus, invoked to sing

characters.name: Mother of the Gods
aliases: mother of all gods and men
characters.description: goddess who loves rattles, timbrels, flutes and wild beasts' cries

analysis.text: The hymn presents the Mother as a goddess of wild nature and ecstatic music, linking beasts, mountains and instruments in her worship.
The rattles, timbrels and flutes reflect the noisy music of the Phrygian Great Mother cult, which came to Greece from Asia Minor.

fun_facts.text: This short hymn is only six lines long, making it one of the briefest in the Homeric collection.

language_notes.text: "I prithee" is archaic for "I pray thee": a polite, urgent request addressed to the Muse.
Timbrels are small hand drums or tambourines, typical of the music of the Mother's worship.
"Coombes" are short, deep valleys or hollows on hillsides.

context_notes.text: The Mother of the gods is Cybele, a Phrygian goddess later identified with Rhea. Her cult featured noisy, ecstatic music and mountain wildness.
Hymns typically end with a farewell to the deity, often asking her favor and promising to remember her in later song.

literary_notes.text: The poet addresses the Muse directly, asking her to sing; this is the conventional invocation opening an epic or hymn.
A list of sounds and wild places, rattles, flutes, wolves, lions and echoing hills, evokes the goddess's untamed, ecstatic nature.
